full_judgment:
Chowdhury A.T.M. Masud, J:—This appeal, by special leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 21.8.82 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka, in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 89 of 1981, dismissing the appeal, but modifying the penalty imposed on the appellant to the extent of his suspension from practice for 5 years from date. By the judgment and order dated 17.12.80 passed by the Bangladesh Bar Council Tribunal No. IV in case No. 13 of 1977 the name of the appellant was removed from the Roll of Advocates for ever. 

 2. The case against the appellant, which started on a petition of complaint lodged with the Bangladesh Bar Council by respondent No.1, Md. Iskandar Ali, is that he came to know appellant Rezaul Karim, an Advocate of Dhaka Court, through his brother-in-law Azizur Rahman who had earlier engaged him in a case. He paid Tk. 5,000/- to the appellant for purchasing 5 kathas of land at Paschim Raza Bazar, P.S. Tejgaon, Dhaka. The land was purchased in the name of the wife of the complainant and 4 others. On the advice of appellant Rezaul Karim, a suit was filed in the First Court of Munsif, Dhaka, being Title Suit No. 299 of 1972 for perfecting the vendees' title and he was engaged as a lawyer for conducting the suit. Due to his negligence the suit was dismissed for default on 12.2.73. The appellant however filed an application under Order 9, Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the case and affirmed affidavit on behalf of all the plaintiffs. Subsequently he filed a suit being Title Suit No. 153 of 1973 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, in the name of his friend Rehanuddin for declaration that the properties in question, the subject matter of earlier Title Suit No. 299 of 1972, were Rehanuddin's benami properties and the vendees were his name-lenders. Plaintiffs Nos. 8, 13, 18, 19 and 20 of the earlier suit were impleaded as defendants in Title Suit No. 153 of 1973. The appellant managed to obtain an exparte decree on 7.9.73 in the name of Rehanuddin. Under the cover of the decree the complainant was ousted from the possession of the suit land. Subsequently the complainant had to file Title Suit No. 195 of 1976 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, for cancellation of the fraudulent and collusive decree passed in Title Suit No. 153 of 1973. He also instituted a criminal case at Kotwali Police Station, Dhaka which is pending for disposal. 

 Respondent No. 1 examined 5 witnesses whereas the appellant examined 3 witnesses at the trial. The Tribunal by a judgment and order dated 17.12.83 found the appellant guilty of gross professional misconduct and removed the name of the appellant from the Roll of Advocates for ever. 

 6. Against the aforesaid judgment and order of the High Court Division, the appellant filed the present appeal by special leave. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's contentions that (1) Professional misconduct has not been defined any where in law or rules and as such the charge of professional misconduct against the appellant was determined arbitrarily by the Tribunal, 2. The finding that the appellant was engaged as an Advocate in Title Suit 

 7. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the appellant argues that the appellant was not an engaged Advocate and even if the allegations against him are accepted he could not be found guilty for professional misconduct. Moreover he argues that professional misconduct has not been defined in statute or rules. 

 9. It is the consistent evidence of the prosecution witnesses that on the advice of the appellant Title Suit No. 299 of 1972 was filed to perfect the title of the vendees and fees and other incidental costs were paid by the plaintiffs to the appellant whom they knew to be their lawyer and he was entrusted with the conduct of their suit. If he did not sign the vokalatnama or if he engaged another lawyer it was not within the knowledge nor with the consent of the plaintiffs. It is also in evidence that the suit was dismissed for default and the appellant swore an affidavit in the miscellaneous case under Order 9, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit. 

 12. The High Court Division and the Tribunal concurrently found that there was conflict of interest between the two suits, namely, Title Suit No. 299 of 1972 led by the complainant and others and the subsequent Title Suit No. 153 of 1973. The appellant obtained an exparte decree in the subsequent suit which was apparently against the interest of the complainant and other plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 299 of 1972 and the acceptance of brief in Title Suit No. 153 of 1973 by the appellant in the facts and circumstances of the case clearly amounts to professional misconduct. There is no substance in the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that professional misconduct has no where been defined and as such the allegation even if established against the appellant could not bring him under the mischief of professional misconduct. Even if the expression 'professional misconduct' has not been defined in the statute or rules, the expression has got a well recognised meaning. In Chapter II of the Canons of Professional Conduct and Etiquetee, adopted under Article 44(g) of P.O. No. 46 of 1972, under the hearing "conduct with regard to clients." it has been provided as follows :- 

 13. In the instant case the High Court Division and the Tribunal concurrently found that the appellant was engaged lawyer of the complainant and he accepted fees for conducting the suit and that there was conflicting interest between their suit and that of the subsequent suit. These findings of fact are based on exhaustive consideration of entire evidence. The learned Counsel for the appellant having found it difficult to effectively challenge the aforesaid finding of facts arrived at the Courts below, argues that in any view of the matter, the penalty imposed is severe. The Tribunal removed the name of the appellant from the Roll of Advocates forever, but the High Court Division has reduced the penalty and suspended the appellant from practice for a period of 5 years only.
